domain: ISC2 Certified in Cybersecurity — Domain 1: Security Principles

content.title: Control Types: Technical, Administrative, Physical

prequestion.prompt: Before reading: a CCTV camera in the server room. Is it a physical control or a detective one?

content.reading_markdown:
## Two questions, not one

Every safeguard can be described two ways, and confusing them is the classic Domain 1 trap.

- **Type** asks *how the control does its job* — through technology, through people and process, or through the physical world.
- **Function** asks *when it acts* — before, during or after the event.

A CCTV camera is a **physical** control by type and both **deterrent** and **detective** by function. Neither answer is wrong; they answer different questions. When an exam item asks for the *type*, give the type.

## The three types

- **Technical** (also called *logical*) — enforced by technology, with no human in the loop at the moment of enforcement: firewalls, encryption, access-control lists, antivirus, MFA systems.
- **Administrative** (also called *managerial*) — the rules that govern people and process: policies, procedures, security awareness training, background checks, separation of duties.
- **Physical** — protects the tangible world and controls access to bodies and hardware: locks, fences, guards, bollards, mantraps.

## The functions, briefly

**Preventive** stops it happening. **Detective** notices that it happened. **Corrective** fixes it afterwards. **Deterrent** discourages the attempt. **Compensating** stands in when the control you really wanted is not feasible.

## Why the split matters

Strong security uses all three types together — this is **defence in depth**. Each type fails differently, so each covers the others' blind spots. The best firewall in the world does not stop someone walking out of the building with a server, and the strongest lock does not stop a phished password.

## Worked example

Protecting a server room takes all three. A least-privilege **policy** decides who may enter at all (administrative). A locked door enforces it against bodies (physical). Full-disk **encryption** on the servers means that even a stolen drive gives up nothing (technical). Remove any one of the three and there is an obvious way in.

gate.prompt: Sort each control by its TYPE — how it does its job. Ignore when it acts; that is its function, not its type.
hints: Ask what an attacker would have to defeat to get past it: logic running in software or hardware, a policy or process the organisation imposes on people, or a physical obstacle.

A control's type doesn't follow from what it protects. Something guarding a computer may be enforced by people, and something guarding a building may be enforced by software. Classify by the enforcer, never by the asset.

Technical: A firewall filtering inbound traffic by rule
Administrative: An acceptable-use policy signed by every employee
Background checks run before a new hire starts
Physical: A perimeter fence around the data centre
A locked door on the server room

gate.accessible_equivalent: Keyboard-navigable list pairing each control with one of {Technical, Administrative, Physical}; scored identically as bucket_assignment.

analog_synthesis.prompt: Away from the screen, pick one room or system you can actually see — your home office, a car, a bike lock, a shared flat. On paper, list every safeguard protecting it and label each one technical, administrative or physical. Then find the gap: which of the three types has no entry at all, and what would you add to fill it?
analog_synthesis.calibration_question: Before checking: did you label anything by *when* it acts (preventive, detective) instead of by *how* it works — and which of the three types did you find yourself with nothing to write against?
analog_synthesis.accessible_equivalent: Describe the same room aloud, listing each safeguard and its type, as a recorded or transcribed spoken response.

drills.prompt: Complete: A control enforced by technology is ______. A control that is a rule people follow is ______. A control that stops a body reaching the hardware is ______.
drills.accessible_equivalent: The same three prompts as a screen-reader accessible select-one list drawn from {technical, administrative, physical, compensating}.
drills.explanation: Technical is also called logical, and administrative is also called managerial — both names appear in the exam outline.

drills.prompt: A new branch office is opening. Select every safeguard on the plan that is an ADMINISTRATIVE control.

correct_set: Annual security awareness training for all staff
Separation of duties on payment approvals
A mandatory data-classification scheme staff must apply to new documents
distractors: A badge-operated turnstile in the lobby
A safe for storing backup tapes
TLS on the customer web portal

drills.accessible_equivalent: Multi-select list with screen-reader labels; scored identically as set_f1.
drills.explanation: Training, procedures, separation of duties and background checks all work by governing what people do. The turnstile and the safe are physical; antivirus and TLS are technical.

drills.prompt: Without notes: name the three control types with two examples of each; explain how a control's type differs from its function; and say why using all three types together is stronger than doubling up on the one you are best at.
drills.accessible_equivalent: Spoken response transcribed via speech-to-text and scored on the same keyword set.
drills.explanation: Being able to say unprompted that type and function are different axes — and that each type fails differently, which is what makes defence in depth work — is the marker that this is a reasoning tool rather than three memorised lists.
